title: Prototyping with AI
tagline: Go from spec to a clickable prototype outline without waiting on an engineer.
intro: You don't need to know how to code to get a prototype in front of people this week. What you need is the same PM skill from Week 2 — a structured prompt — pointed at describing screens and states instead of describing a tool call.

scenario.context: The Onboarding Packet Agent's guardrail file from Week 3 is written. Now design and engineering need to see roughly what the HR rep's side of the conversation looks like before committing real build time. (The same outline-first approach applies to any Employer Services admin tool — an Unemployment Cost Management claims-review dashboard would start from the same three questions: what does the admin see, what can they change, and what's the one moment worth testing first.)
scenario.brief: Outline a 3-screen flow for the HR rep's view of the Onboarding Packet Agent: (1) the request and the agent's interpreted match, shown for confirmation before anything sends, (2) the packet contents for that batch, with any hire-type exceptions flagged, (3) the send-status screen once the HR rep confirms.

sections.heading: Screen 1 — Request & match preview
sections.learning: Describe states, not just layout. 'A text box and a button' is a layout. 'A matched-employee list that's empty until the agent finishes interpreting the request, with each row showing exactly why it matched' is a prototype outline an AI tool can actually build something useful from.

example.text: HR rep's typed request at the top, shown verbatim. Below it, the agent's interpreted criteria as a plain-language chip (e.g., 'Start date Nov 1–30 · 6 matches') so the rep can catch a misread date range at a glance. Below that, the matched new hires in a simple table — name, site, start date — with nothing sent yet.

sections.pitfall: Showing the matched list without showing how the request was interpreted. If the HR rep can't see 'Nov 1–30' next to '6 matches,' they can't catch a misread date range before it turns into six misdirected packets — the interpretation has to be visible, not just the result.

field.label: Your turn: Screen 1
field.help: What does the HR rep see after typing a request, before anything is sent?
field.placeholder: Describe the layout and, importantly, its states.

sections.heading: Screen 2 — Packet contents & exceptions
sections.learning: What can the HR rep change, and how are hire-type exceptions surfaced before send, not after?

example.text: The standard six-form packet listed once, with a note showing it applies to all 6 matched hires except one — a rehire, flagged with 'Rehire: confirm which forms apply' requiring the HR rep to check or uncheck forms for that one person specifically before the batch can be confirmed.

sections.pitfall: Applying the standard packet to everyone silently, including the one hire-type exception the agent's rules don't cover. An exception that's buried instead of flagged inline means the HR rep only finds out after several people got forms that didn't apply to them.

field.label: Your turn: Screen 2
field.help: How are the packet contents shown, and how are exceptions (like a rehire) surfaced?
field.placeholder: Describe the editable states and what gets flagged.

sections.heading: Screen 3 — Send status
sections.learning: What does the HR rep see once they've confirmed and the agent has actually sent the packets?

example.text: A per-employee status line — Sent, or a specific reason it wasn't (bounced email, missing address) — so a batch of 40 doesn't just report 'Done' with no way to tell if 3 silently failed. Anything that didn't send routes to a clear next action, not a dead end.

sections.pitfall: Showing one aggregate 'Packets sent!' message instead of per-employee status. A single success banner hides the one delivery failure in a batch of 40 that actually needs someone to notice and fix it before that person's Day 1.

field.label: Your turn: Screen 3
field.help: What does the HR rep see after sending, and how are failures surfaced?
field.placeholder: Describe the status view and what happens for a failed send.

sections.heading: Key interaction, in depth
sections.learning: One key interaction beats three flat screens. Pick the single most important moment — usually where the user makes a decision or the AI hands control back to a human — and describe it in more depth than everything else. That's usually the part worth testing with real people first.

example.text: The confirmation moment (Screen 1 into Screen 2) is the one worth testing first — it's where we learn whether HR reps actually read the interpreted criteria and matched list before confirming, or whether they click through on habit, which would mean the confirmation step isn't really providing the safety it's designed for.

sections.pitfall: Picking the interaction that's easiest to prototype instead of the one that's riskiest to be wrong about. A polished send-status screen doesn't tell you anything you didn't already know — the confirmation moment does.

field.label: Your turn: Key interaction
field.help: Pick the single most important moment and describe it in more depth than the screens above.
field.placeholder: Name the moment and why it's the one worth testing first.

sections.heading: The prompt you'd use to generate this
sections.learning: Write the actual prompt you'd type into Claude or Gemini to turn this outline into a first-pass mockup or clickable flow.

example.text: Act as a product designer. Generate a 3-screen wireframe description for an HR rep tool with these screens and states: [paste the three screens above]. Output as a numbered list of UI elements per screen, no visual design opinions yet.

sections.pitfall: Asking the AI to also make visual design decisions ('make it look nice') in the same prompt as the structural outline. Separate 'what elements exist and what state are they in' from 'what it looks like' — mixing the two produces a prototype that's polished but structurally wrong.

field.label: Your turn: Prompt
field.help: Write the prompt you'd use to generate a first-pass mockup from this outline.
